source: Written for Wayword as a learner's guide; not part of the original dataset. Examples are dataset phrases.
intro: European Portuguese swallows its unstressed vowels and turns final s into sh. That's why it sounds almost Slavic next to Spanish, and why Brazilians can sound so different.
reading: "uh" and "oo" at the end of a word are short and weak: POH-duh, oh-bree-GAH-doo.

An "n" or "ng" after a vowel (kohn, bohn, nowng, seeng, kong) usually just means that vowel is nasal: say it through your nose and don't actually pronounce the n or g. "Com" is a nasal "koh", whether it's spelled kohn or kong.

The pronunciation line is the slow, careful version, one word at a time. Real speech (and the recording) is faster: words run together and short vowels shrink or vanish. Read the line to learn the sounds, then copy the rhythm from the recording. Where the two differ a lot, the phrase has a "How it's said" tip.

sounds.name: Swallowed vowels
sounds.how: An unstressed e shrinks to a faint "uh" or disappears; an unstressed o becomes "oo". Pode is "POH-duh", obrigado ends in "doo".

sounds.name: Nasal vowels
sounds.how: Let the vowel resonate through your nose and stop before a full m or n. Não is one nasal glide, "nowng".

sounds.name: S at the end of a syllable
sounds.how: At the end of a syllable or word, s (and z) becomes sh, or zh before a voiced sound: está is "esh-TAH", inglês is "een-GLAYSH". Most of Brazil keeps it as s.

sounds.name: Words run together
sounds.how: Portuguese speakers don't pause between words. A final s before a vowel turns into z and joins the next word (Estados Unidos is "esh-TAH-du-zoo-NEE-dush"). A weak final e disappears into the next vowel, and a final o before a vowel turns into a quick w. If the recording seems to skip a sound, this is usually why.

sounds.name: NH and LH
sounds.how: nh = ny as in "canyon"; lh = lli as in "million".

sounds.name: Two r sounds
sounds.how: Between vowels, r is a quick tap like the tt in American "butter". At the start of a word, and when doubled, it's throaty in Lisbon, close to a French r.

sounds.name: Soft consonants
sounds.how: ch = sh. j, and g before e or i, = zh as in "measure". ç, and c before e or i, = s.

tips_source: "How it's said" tips are written for Wayword (not part of the dataset): how a Lisbon speaker says the phrase at normal speed, next to the careful pronunciation line.

tips.how_are_you: Said quickly, the e of está is often dropped: KOH-moo shTAH.
tips.how_say: Diz ends in sh, not z (a final z sounds like sh): KOH-moo suh DEESH.
tips.say_again: Pode loses its final e, and the first e of repetir almost vanishes: POHD rpuh-TEER. The r at the start is the throaty one.
tips.dont_understand: The e in per- nearly disappears: nowng pr-SEH-boo.
tips.what_mean: The que's are short and weak, "kuh", and the whole start runs together: oo-kee-EH-kuh EE-soo kehr dee-ZEHR.
tips.whats_in_this: The start runs together into one word, oo-kee-EH-kuh, with weak "kuh" sounds.
tips.what_do_you_do: Faz ends in sh (a final z sounds like sh), and que is a weak "kuh": oo kuh FAHSH.
tips.recommend_food: Que is a weak "kuh" here: oo kuh ruh-koo-MEN-dah.
tips.learning_language: Estou often drops its first e (shTOH), and "a aprender" blurs into one long "ah": shTOH-ah-pren-DEHR.
tips.learning_by_trying: Estou often drops its first e (shTOH), and "a aprender" blurs into one long "ah".
tips.im_visiting: Estou often drops its first e, and de shrinks to just d: shTOH d'vee-ZEE-tah.
tips.is_far: The final e of longe is barely there: eh LONZH.
tips.help_me: The final -me is almost just m: POHD ah-zhoo-DARM.
tips.bathroom: De shrinks to a quick d: ON-duh FEE-kah ah KAH-zah d'BAN-yoo.
tips.how_get: Chego and a join, the o turning into a quick w: KOH-moo SHEH-gwah.
tips.where_from: De and onde join up: DON-duh eh.
tips.live_here: Vive loses its final e and joins aqui: VEEV-ah-KEE.
tips.im_new_here: Novo and aqui join, the o turning into a quick w: soh NOH-vwah-KEE.
tips.been_america: In normal speech the s of Estados joins Unidos as a z, and the short vowels around it shrink: esh-TAH-du-zoo-NEE-dush. The recording says it this way, so it can sound like a syllable is missing.
tips.love_languages: Adoro and aprender join, the o turning into a quick w: ah-DOH-rwah-pren-DEHR.
tips.like_talking: Gosto's final o is weak, and de shrinks to a quick d: GOSH-too d'fah-LAR.
tips.interesting: Que and interessante run together, and the final e almost vanishes: keen-tuh-ruh-SANT.
tips.tip_included: Está often drops its first e: ah goor-ZHEH-tah shTAH een-kloo-EE-dah.
